<p class="cycle-role">Existing knowledge and its relevance across places.</p>

<p class="page-deck"><strong>How does place shape which urban climate knowledge is produced, recognised and useful elsewhere?</strong></p>

Cities rarely possess complete local evidence for every climate decision, so they draw on studies, cases, models and practical experience produced elsewhere. Yet the relevance of that knowledge depends on more than geographical proximity or superficial similarity. Institutional arrangements, infrastructure, climate, political authority, data systems and social conditions may all affect whether a finding remains useful in another setting.

This theme studies the geography of urban climate knowledge: where evidence is produced, which cities and populations are made visible, how particular cases become reference points, and under what conditions findings may inform decisions beyond their original location. We examine not only whether knowledge travels, but also how it is interpreted, adapted, combined or rejected as it moves between places.

::: {.notice}
**Analytical boundary.** This theme concerns existing knowledge and the conditions under which it may be relevant elsewhere. It does not assume that findings transfer unchanged between cities.

**Place in the learning cycle.** Mapping the reach and limits of existing knowledge reveals which unresolved questions could be consequential enough to justify new research.
:::

## Questions the lab investigates

- Where is urban climate knowledge produced, recognised and made visible?
- Which cities can plausibly learn from one another, and under what conditions?
- How do institutional and geographic contexts shape replication, comparison and case-study usefulness?

<div class="idea-grid"><article class="idea-card"><p class="idea-disclaimer">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Under what conditions can findings produced in one city inform a decision in another?</h3><p>Clearer conditions for relevance could help cities use external evidence without assuming that it transfers unchanged.</p><h4>Suggested methods</h4><ul class="method-list"><li>transportability and generalisability</li><li>hierarchical meta analysis</li><li>matched city comparison</li><li>city typologies</li><li>geospatial analysis</li></ul></article><article class="idea-card"><p class="idea-disclaimer">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Which cities and populations are structurally absent from influential urban climate evidence?</h3><p>Systematic absence may narrow what is treated as general knowledge and leave important conditions invisible to research and policy.</p><h4>Suggested methods</h4><ul class="method-list"><li>bibliometric mapping</li><li>natural language processing</li><li>geocoding</li><li>citation network analysis</li><li>population vulnerability comparison</li></ul></article><article class="idea-card"><p class="idea-disclaimer">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>How is evidence changed as it moves through city networks, intermediary organisations and policy institutions?</h3><p>Tracing adaptation and reuse could show why apparently shared evidence produces different understandings across institutions and places.</p><h4>Suggested methods</h4><ul class="method-list"><li>comparative process tracing</li><li>policy document analysis</li><li>interviews</li><li>network analysis</li><li>citation and document reuse tracing</li></ul></article></div>

## Connections across the learning cycle

- **Input from [Consequences for People and Places](/research/consequences-for-people-and-places.html):** Observed consequences generate new knowledge, expose the limits of earlier assumptions and change what other cities may plausibly learn.
- **Next stage — [Where New Evidence Matters](/research/where-new-evidence-matters.html):** Mapping the reach and limits of existing knowledge reveals which unresolved questions could be consequential enough to justify new research.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
